gdpr-ai-chatbots-schools.title: AI in school: the questions to ask before anyone pastes pupil data
gdpr-ai-chatbots-schools.excerpt: A practical starting point for heads, business managers and DPOs reviewing an AI tool.
gdpr-ai-chatbots-schools.body:
A member of staff has found a tool that turns a long document into a useful summary. It saves time. Then someone asks whether it could summarise an annual review. That is the point to pause and check what has changed.

A public policy and a child's education, health and care plan do not carry the same risks. A sensible school AI policy helps colleagues recognise that difference before they upload anything.

Start with the task, not the badge

The DfE advises schools to understand how an AI tool uses personal data and involve their data protection officer. A supplier saying it is secure does not explain the particular service, account type and settings your staff will use.

Write down the job in one sentence. Could a general letter about collection arrangements be drafted without names or individual circumstances? Give staff a useful approved example, rather than leaving them with a policy that only says be careful.

Ask specific questions

  • What information is sent, including uploads and conversation history?
  • Which organisations process it, and in which countries?
  • How long is it retained, including logs and backups?
  • Is it used for model training, and do the terms match our account?
  • How can the school delete information, control access and report an incident?

Ask your DPO to help establish the lawful basis, contracts and whether a data protection impact assessment is required. Keep the answers with the approval decision.

A parent chatbot needs boundaries too

Public information can become a private conversation. A parent asking about uniform is one thing; someone describing a safeguarding concern is another. Decide what the chatbot should answer, when it directs someone to staff and how urgent concerns are handled. Test those situations before launch.

Check answers against published information. Test a wrong premise, an old date and a question the website cannot answer. A confident invention is worse than a clear admission that someone needs to help.

Make the safe route the easy route

Our suggestion is a one-page staff guide: approved tools, allowed tasks, prohibited information, who reviews outputs and who to ask. Review it when the product or its terms change. Keep professional decisions with the people accountable for them.

Ask those questions of Schoolgle as well. Our data protection hub starts a product-specific review. This is practical guidance for schools in England, not approval to share a particular dataset.

preparing-for-ofsted-2025.title: Ofsted in September 2026: update the right things, avoid extra paperwork
preparing-for-ofsted-2025.excerpt: What the current inspection materials change, what they do not require, and a focused way for leaders to review their school’s next steps.
preparing-for-ofsted-2025.source: Ofsted: current toolkit, change summary and inspection information
summary: Use the toolkit version for inspections from 7 September 2026.
Do not create written evidence against every standard or an inspection-only SEF.
Review the relevant changes through existing school processes and retain the decisions.

sources.title: State-funded school inspection toolkit
sources.published: June 2026, version 2.0; for inspections from 7 September 2026

sources.title: School inspection: toolkit, operating guides and information
Summary of changes
sources.published: Updated 28 August 2026; June and August 2026 changes distinguished

sources.title: Inspection information for state-funded schools
sources.published: Updated 28 August 2026; for inspections from 7 September 2026

preparing-for-ofsted-2025.body:
Schools in England need to update the inspection references they use this September. They do not need to create an inspection-only version of everyday school life. This briefing separates the confirmed changes from a practical review a leadership team could complete without commissioning another evidence collection exercise.

Our source check was completed on 7 September 2026. The official state-funded school inspection toolkit identifies itself as June 2026, version 2.0, for inspections from 7 September. The supporting publication collection was updated again on 28 August. Those dates describe different documents, rather than two competing start dates.

What the September update actually changes

Ofsted's summary of changes separates June's toolkit revisions from August's later clarifications. June's list includes comparison of attainment and progress with similar schools, disadvantaged pupils and pupils with SEND, inclusion and family engagement, mobile phone policies, and several safeguarding and early years matters. It also identifies changes to operating and monitoring guidance. This is a range of clarifications across documents, not a single new school checklist.

The August additions concern reasons for a category-of-concern decision and inspectors' access to DBS-related information for volunteers in regulated activity. Schools should check the full wording and relevant responsibilities. An update about access to records should not be turned into a blanket instruction to repeat every check.

What leaders should not manufacture

The toolkit describes inspection as an evaluation of how the school ordinarily works, using first-hand evidence and professional conversations. Required documentation should relate to statutory responsibilities or normal school business; inspectors do not require a special presentation format. That gives leaders a useful test for every proposed preparation task: does this improve our work, or merely repackage it for visitors?

The current inspection information for schools is more explicit about common misconceptions. It does not require written evidence against every toolkit standard or a formal written self-evaluation. It does not prescribe a planning format, grade individual teachers or lessons, or specify the volume of marking. It also states that schools are not expected to use AI. These limits should travel with the update when it is shared with staff.

A focused leadership review

The following is Schoolgle's suggested working routine, not an additional Ofsted requirement. Ask one leader to bring the existing improvement priorities and another to bring the official change summary. Discuss where a change affects something the school actually does. Record a decision only where there is something to clarify, correct or follow up.

  • Identify the current source and the relevant paragraph. Avoid acting on a social-media paraphrase alone.
  • Name the existing school process it touches, such as volunteer arrangements or a family-engagement review.
  • Decide whether practice already addresses it. If so, note the reason rather than inventing another action.
  • Where work is needed, give it an owner, a proportionate next step and a review date.
  • Tell staff what they can stop producing, as well as what needs attention.

Keep the record somewhere the team already uses. A short decision in an ordinary meeting can be more useful than a new tracker that nobody owns. Revisit unfinished actions through the same leadership routine.

Make a school judgement possible to question

For a priority involving reading, our suggested discussion begins with the exact claim. Does it concern decoding, understanding a text, a particular year group or a defined group of pupils? Put the period and assessment method beside it. A national test result, a teacher's assessment and a short intervention check are different sources and should remain distinguishable.

Then ask what would challenge the explanation. A change in the pupils included, missing assessments or a different task could affect the apparent pattern. Invite the colleague closest to the teaching to explain those details. An attractive chart should not make uncertainty harder to see.

Choose one existing action and trace it through: what prompted it, what happened, what evidence followed and what leaders decided. If the trail ends at attendance at training, the team still needs a question about classroom use and pupil learning. A weak or mixed result is a reason to investigate, not to rewrite the original claim.

Use technology for the record, not the verdict

A shared system can help locate sources and retain ownership, dates and decisions. A supplier's completed checklist or generated narrative cannot establish an inspection grade. Before adding software, identify the actual task it would improve and ask colleagues to demonstrate that workflow with appropriately controlled information.

Use the official documents for the applicable inspection process and standards. This briefing concerns state-funded school inspection in England; other settings and UK nations have their own arrangements. The practical routines above are editorial suggestions, not an inspection-readiness certification.

eef-teaching-learning-toolkit-guide.title: Using the EEF Toolkit without turning it into a shopping list
eef-teaching-learning-toolkit-guide.excerpt: Start with a pupil need, examine the evidence and plan a manageable change.
eef-teaching-learning-toolkit-guide.body:
It is tempting to open the EEF Toolkit, find a promising approach and announce a priority. The difficult bit starts on Monday, when someone has to fit that approach into an actual lesson.

The Toolkit summarises research on teaching and learning approaches. It starts an informed decision; it is not a menu of guaranteed gains.

Describe the need first

Pupils struggle with reading is too broad. A group can decode accurately but struggles to explain unfamiliar text gives the team something to investigate. Check classroom evidence, speak to teachers and explore competing explanations. Keep the inquiry open long enough to avoid choosing the intervention you already wanted to buy.

Read beyond the headline

Look at evidence strength, costs and implementation considerations. An average across studies is not a forecast for your class. Do not treat estimates as precise targets or add gains from several approaches together.

Ask what staff need to do differently. Which parts are essential? What knowledge, resources and practice will they need? Which existing activity will make room for the change?

Plan the work after the launch

The EEF's implementation guidance describes Explore, Prepare, Deliver and Sustain. Our suggestion is a short record: the pupil need, the approach, the reason for choosing it, staff support and a review plan.

Review delivery as well as outcomes. An approach rarely used because training was missing is a different finding from an approach implemented well without the hoped-for effect. Both deserve honest discussion.

Collect evidence you will use

A work sample, focused assessment and staff observations may be more useful than a dashboard full of measures nobody needs. Record whether you will continue, adapt or stop, and why.

Schoolgle can connect an improvement action to its evidence and review. The professional choice remains with the school.

hse-school-compliance-gap.title: School compliance: close the gap between a check and the follow-up
hse-school-compliance-gap.excerpt: A completed form is only useful if someone acts on what it found.
hse-school-compliance-gap.body:
The check happened. Someone recorded a problem. A contractor was contacted. Three weeks later, nobody is quite sure whether the work was finished. That gap is worth attention.

The DfE's Good Estate Management guidance covers responsibilities, planning and maintaining the estate. Use it to review your arrangements. Can a concern be followed from discovery to resolution?

Give the issue a next step

Our suggested record is simple: what was checked, when, by whom, what was found and what happens next. Link evidence where appropriate. Give an action an owner and a review date. Reported should not be the end of the story.

Agree who escalates unresolved issues and when, reflecting the risk and competent advice. A dashboard colour cannot substitute for a professional assessment.

Separate requirements from routines

Not every useful check has the same legal basis or frequency. Arrangements need to reflect the premises, risk assessments and relevant advice. A checklist copied from another school may omit something important or add work that does not fit your site.

Keep the basis for a routine alongside it. That helps when a contractor recommends a change or a new site manager asks why the school does things this way.

Test the handover

Choose one completed job and one overdue job. Ask a colleague who was not involved to find the history, current owner and evidence. If they cannot, improve the record before creating another report.

Schoolgle's Estates workflow brings recurring checks, jobs and completion evidence together. It does not replace specialist advice or the school's legal duties.

school-building-condition-crisis.title: School estates in autumn 2026: what the new return changes
school-building-condition-crisis.excerpt: The first estates standards return is approaching. Who submits it, what condition surveys establish, and how schools can turn records into a practical action programme.
summary: Confirm your responsible body and the route for school input before the autumn return.
Record survey scope and unresolved questions alongside the action programme.
Use consistent, dated building records to prepare for the planned data changes.

sources.title: School estate management standards annual return
Condition surveys for school and college buildings: guidance for responsible bodies
Education Estates Strategy: a decade of national renewal

school-building-condition-crisis.body:
For school leaders in England, this autumn brings a specific estates task alongside the familiar repairs list: helping the organisation responsible for their buildings give an honest account of how the estate is managed. The useful question is whether a reported problem can be followed through to a decision, an owner and a verified outcome. A folder full of certificates cannot answer that by itself.

This briefing separates the current Department for Education position from Schoolgle's suggested way to organise the work. It is reviewed on 7 September 2026; dates described as forthcoming are still forthcoming at that point.

The September change: know who submits

DfE's annual return starts this academic year. Its guidance, updated on 10 August, asks responsible bodies eligible for annual DfE capital funding to submit; individual schools do not submit separately. The published window opens in the third week of September and closes in late November. It uses multiple-choice questions without supporting-document uploads. DfE says responses will not affect funding, and organisations are expected to work towards level 3, rather than all already meet it. Read the current annual-return guidance for access and submission arrangements.

For a school business manager, the first conversation is therefore with the relevant trust, local authority or diocese. Agree who needs the school's input and when. A single-academy trust should check its responsible-body role rather than assume the individual-school wording removes its involvement. Avoid creating a second questionnaire merely because the national return is new.

A condition survey has a defined job

DfE's February 2026 commissioning guidance describes a condition survey as a visual, non-intrusive inspection by an independent, qualified professional. It is not a structural survey; concealed areas are not opened unless included in the scope. Responsible bodies should commission comprehensive surveys at least every five years, with earlier surveys where concerns justify them. The page describes itself as interim guidance ahead of new technical standards. Check the commissioning guidance and its current status when preparing a brief.

The practical implication is to record both what a report establishes and what it leaves unanswered. In a fictional school, a ceiling stain reappears after a repair. The old survey, a contractor's invoice and a photograph are three different pieces of information. None, alone, establishes why the stain returned. Log the recurrence, identify the appropriate competent adviser and document the resulting action. An urgent concern belongs in the school's immediate escalation arrangements; it should not wait for a scheduled reporting cycle.

Prepare a small pack that supports decisions

Schoolgle's suggested starting pack is deliberately short. It should make uncertainty visible and let someone who was not present at the last meeting understand what happens next:

  • A site and building list with the responsible organisation and a named operational contact.
  • A survey register showing date, scope, location of the original report and outstanding questions.
  • A prioritised action list distinguishing an observation, professional advice, an approved decision and completed work.
  • A forward programme showing dependencies, provisional costs, funding status and the next review point.

Use links to the original records where they already live. Avoid copying a report into several folders and leaving colleagues to guess which version applies. Give each open item an owner, but also record who has authority to approve the work. Those can be different people, especially where the school occupies buildings owned or managed by another organisation.

For the recurring leak example, a useful closure record might say which defect was addressed, who checked the repair and when the next inspection will happen. An invoice confirms a transaction; a closed task should explain the outcome. This is an editorial workflow example, not a claim about any named school or a substitute for specialist assessment.

Connect this term's work to the longer direction

The February Education Estates Strategy sets out a ten-year direction. It plans data-collection pilots in 2026–27, national rollout from autumn 2027 and two-way data sharing by 2028. Those are programme milestones, not evidence that every school already uses a common system. They make consistent building identifiers, dated records and exportable information sensible preparation.

At the next estates meeting, choose one unresolved issue and trace it from first report to present position. If the team cannot explain the evidence, decision and next step, repair that process before expanding the dashboard. The aim is a clearer route from concern to action, with a defensible record of what remains uncertain and why.

metacognition-self-regulation-schools.title: Metacognition in practice: what the updated EEF guidance means for teaching
metacognition-self-regulation-schools.excerpt: Go beyond a reflection box: examine the evidence, teach a purposeful strategy and check what pupils can do when the support changes.
metacognition-self-regulation-schools.source: EEF: metacognition, Toolkit, feedback and implementation guidance
summary: The verified guidance is the second edition published in November 2025.
The Toolkit’s average impact is not a promise for a programme or pupil.
Examine a new task, the support used and the pupil’s explanation before claiming independence.

sources.title: Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning
Metacognition and self-regulation: Teaching and Learning Toolkit
Teacher Feedback to Improve Pupil Learning
A School’s Guide to Implementation
A structured, but flexible, implementation process
sources.published: Part of the third edition, published 24 April 2024

metacognition-self-regulation-schools.body:
A pupil completes a task correctly after several prompts. That is useful information, but it leaves an important question: what will the pupil choose to do when the prompts are absent? Metacognition becomes practical when teachers can identify that decision, teach an approach and look for its use on another task.

The EEF's second-edition guidance was published on 13 November 2025. It is the edition verified for this briefing on 7 September 2026, not a new 2026 research finding. It develops recommendations for primary and secondary schools and is aimed particularly at teachers and leaders supporting professional development.

What the updated guidance asks teachers to teach

The report connects pupils' knowledge of themselves, available strategies and the task with how they direct their learning. It recommends explicit teaching, teacher modelling, purposeful discussion, appropriate challenge and guided practice leading towards independence. These approaches sit within subject teaching: pupils need useful subject knowledge and methods before they can decide which method fits.

Our interpretation is that a reflection sheet cannot carry this work on its own. A pupil needs something specific to notice or change while working. The full report provides the detail behind the recommendations and should be read before adopting a school-wide routine.

Read the impact figure with its limitations

The Toolkit strand, whose evidence review is dated May 2025, reports an average equivalent to eight additional months of progress and identifies 355 studies. It rates the evidence as high, while explaining that many studies were not independently evaluated. Evaluations involving organisations connected to an approach tend to show larger effects, which can influence the overall estimate.

This is evidence about a broad family of teaching approaches, not a forecast for a purchased programme, an individual pupil or a particular school. The Toolkit also notes that practice is difficult to implement well. Its low-cost rating does not remove the need for staff time and professional development. Treat the headline as a reason to examine the approach carefully, not as a target to promise governors.

A classroom example to discuss together

This is an original Schoolgle planning example, not a reported trial. Imagine a class comparing two accounts of the same event. Before reading, ask pupils to decide which question they are trying to answer. Give them a small evidence space with room for a claim, a supporting detail and something the account leaves uncertain.

After the first account, pause. A pupil may have a plausible claim but no supporting detail. Instead of rewarding confidence, ask them to point to the passage their claim depends on. After the second account, invite them to keep, qualify or change the claim and say what prompted that decision.

For the follow-up, use two short accounts of a different event and change the order of presentation. Note whether pupils use evidence without being told which sentence matters. Do not treat a longer answer as automatically better reasoning; a brief, well-supported correction may reveal more.

Give feedback a job to do

The EEF's feedback guidance, published on 11 June 2021, focuses on teacher-delivered feedback. Its recommendations include establishing learning intentions, identifying gaps and planning how pupils will use the feedback. It does not establish that a particular automated hint or game reward has the same effect.

For our classroom example, the useful feedback concerns the missing support for a claim. Leave time for a revision and inspect what changed. Recording that feedback was delivered is different from recording that the pupil acted on it.

Plan a manageable trial of the teaching routine

The EEF's implementation guidance, third edition dated 24 April 2024, treats implementation as work involving people, context and a structured process. Its process guidance covers exploration, preparation, delivery and sustaining an approach. A launch meeting is therefore only one part of the job.

Our suggested starting record has four decisions: the subject task, the pupil difficulty being investigated, the teaching change and the evidence the team will revisit. Choose a review date that fits the teaching sequence. Include what staff need to rehearse and what existing activity will make room for it.

  • Keep an initial response and a later response to a different but comparable task.
  • Record the help actually given, including reading support, modelled examples and hints.
  • Look for pupils who still struggle, rather than allowing a class average to end the discussion.
  • Separate whether the routine was used from whether learning improved.

A digital record can preserve those observations, but it cannot infer a pupil's thinking from clicks alone. Look for an explanation, a purposeful change or successful use on a new task. Review such evidence with the teacher's knowledge of the pupil. This is a proposed evaluation routine, not a claim that Schoolgle has demonstrated improved attainment.

evidence-organisation-before-inspection.title: Evidence organisation: make the useful document easy to find
evidence-organisation-before-inspection.excerpt: Keep sources, owners and review decisions connected.
evidence-organisation-before-inspection.body:
The document exists. Someone remembers discussing it. The difficulty is finding the right version while six other things need attention.

Evidence organisation should support ordinary leadership work: understanding a decision, answering a question or picking up an action. A folder structure nobody maintains will not do that.

Keep a recognisable source

Our suggestion is to agree where the current document lives and link to it from the places that need it. Avoid separate copies for governors, improvement planning and inspection preparation without a clear reason. Copies drift apart quietly.

Give the document a meaningful name, an owner and a review date. Access matters too: the right colleague needs to find it without making sensitive material available to everyone.

Connect it to the question

A link is not an explanation. Add a short note saying why the source matters and which period or group it describes. Distinguish what it shows from what leaders infer. Retain limitations.

A termly attendance summary may support a question about a cohort. It does not automatically explain individual absences. Keep the inquiry proportionate to the source.

Use existing meetings

Check the links for the priority you are discussing. Update ownership and record the next decision. A reliable routine can be more useful than a school-wide filing project.

Check current inspection materials for your setting. Schoolgle connects the school's sources, findings and actions so the evidence can be used throughout the year.

self-evaluation-that-works.title: Self-evaluation that helps leaders decide what to do next
self-evaluation-that-works.excerpt: Keep judgement, evidence and uncertainty close enough to discuss honestly.
self-evaluation-that-works.body:
A self-evaluation can sound polished and still leave a team unsure what to do on Monday. The useful version helps people agree what is working, where evidence is less convincing and what needs attention.

Write a judgement someone can question

Choose a specific area and say what you currently think. Show the evidence and its limits. Avoid starting with an adjective and collecting examples to defend it. The point is to understand the school, including what does not fit the first explanation.

Our suggested discussion has four parts: what we believe, what supports it, what complicates it and what happens next. These work in a meeting note without a new reporting exercise.

Separate activity from effect

Staff attended training describes an activity. Pupils use the strategy independently describes a possible effect that needs evidence. Both matter, but they are not interchangeable.

A strong example from one class may suggest practice to investigate elsewhere. It does not establish that an approach is embedded throughout the school.

Let the account change

When later evidence challenges an earlier view, record the change and the reason. That is useful evaluation, not a failure to tell a consistent story. Keep the previous decision recoverable so the team understands the learning.

Check current inspection materials, but keep self-evaluation rooted in improvement. Schoolgle can organise evidence and actions around that conversation. Judgement belongs to leaders, informed by the people doing the work.

action-plans-that-stay-current.title: Action plans that survive the first half-term
action-plans-that-stay-current.excerpt: A named owner, a sensible review and a clear reason to keep going.
action-plans-that-stay-current.body:
An improvement plan starts with good intentions. Then school life intervenes, and it becomes a document someone updates before a meeting rather than a tool people use.

Make the action small enough to own

Improve writing is a priority, not an action. Agree what someone will do, who it concerns and when it will be reviewed. If several people contribute, make one person responsible for bringing the update back.

Our suggested record holds the baseline, intended change, owner, support and review evidence together. The next conversation should not need to start from scratch.

Plan beyond the launch

The EEF describes implementation through Explore, Prepare, Deliver and Sustain. Ask whether staff understand the approach, have time to practise and know what support is available.

A training date is a milestone. It does not establish that practice changed. Give someone responsibility for noticing the difference.

Close the loop honestly

Ask what happened, what evidence is available and what it means. Continue, adapt or stop for a stated reason. Record constraints and decide whether a delayed action is still a priority.

Do not mark success merely because the activity happened. Equally, do not call an approach ineffective when the conditions for implementation never existed.

Schoolgle connects ownership, evidence and review. Keep priorities manageable enough that people use the plan to make decisions, rather than report busyness.

80-percent-software-features-unused.title: Before the next software renewal, ask what staff actually use
80-percent-software-features-unused.excerpt: A practical review of licences, duplicated work and the support that would help.
80-percent-software-features-unused.body:
The renewal email arrives and the subscription carries on. Meanwhile, one team uses the system daily, another keeps a spreadsheet and nobody is certain which features are included.

You do not need a dramatic national statistic to investigate that. The useful evidence is in your own school. This guide replaces an earlier unsupported school-specific percentage claim; the existing URL is retained for continuity.

Follow one task

Ask a colleague to show you a regular job from beginning to end. Where do they copy information, ask someone for help or export a file? Observe the actual process, including the workarounds.

A little-used feature is not automatically waste. It may serve an important annual task. Equally, frequent logins do not prove that a system saves time.

Make a small renewal record

  • What job does this subscription support?
  • Who uses it, and who owns the renewal?
  • What is the total cost and notice period?
  • Which features overlap with another service?
  • Would training solve the problem more cheaply than replacement?

Speak to staff before deciding. Removing a tool without understanding its role can shift hidden work onto someone else.

Test the improvement

Our suggestion is one change with a before-and-after check: less re-entry, fewer handoffs or a task completed reliably. Keep the measure close to the work.

DfE workload resources provide wider context. Schoolgle's starting point is the same practical question: which task is awkward, and what would make it easier? Bring us that task and we will show you where the product fits.

teacher-workload-technology-gap.title: When technology adds work: start with the duplicate task
teacher-workload-technology-gap.excerpt: A small, staff-led approach to finding out what a new system should remove.
teacher-workload-technology-gap.body:
A new system can make a report look better while leaving the work behind it untouched. Someone still collects the information, checks it and pastes it into another document.

Ask what will stop

Before adding a tool, name the task it will remove or simplify. If the answer is another dashboard, keep asking. A staff member should be able to explain the benefit in terms of their working day.

Our suggested review follows one recurring process. List the inputs, handoffs, checks and outputs. Ask why each step exists. Some are essential; others may survive because nobody had permission to stop them.

Keep staff involved

The DfE maintains workload resources for schools. Use that wider guidance alongside the team's own experience. A technically elegant workflow that ignores the timetable or access arrangements will not help.

Include occasional users and the person who covers absence. A process that works only for its designer has a handover problem.

Measure the whole job

Check time spent preparing, entering and correcting information. Notice whether work moved from a teacher to an administrator rather than disappearing. Review accuracy and whether the output is actually used.

Agree a short trial and a decision date. Keep, adapt or stop the change based on evidence. Schoolgle should earn its place by helping with a real task, not by asking schools to maintain another layer of reporting.

teacher-retention-crisis-2026.title: Teacher retention in 2026: fewer departures, but a smaller FTE workforce
teacher-retention-crisis-2026.excerpt: The June workforce release shows falling departures alongside a lower teacher FTE total. What the different measures mean for staffing decisions this autumn.
teacher-retention-crisis-2026.source: Schoolgle briefing · Department for Education workforce and research releases
summary: Teacher FTE and departure measures cover different populations; read their definitions before comparing them.
Qualifying-cohort retention is different from staying at the same school.
Use national evidence to frame a focused local investigation of capacity and workload.

sources.title: School workforce in England: reporting year 2025
Teacher retention: reporting year 2025 dataset
Initial Teacher Training Census: academic year 2025/26
Working lives of teachers and leaders: wave 4
Working lives wave 4 summary report, RR1578

teacher-retention-crisis-2026.body:
England’s latest workforce figures describe a mixed picture, not a simple story of accelerating departures. For school leaders planning the autumn term, the important question is which pressure they actually face: losing colleagues, reducing contracted hours, or struggling to recruit particular expertise. Those problems need different responses. This Schoolgle briefing separates the national evidence from our suggested approach to local workforce planning.

What the June release actually shows

DfE’s 2025 school workforce release, published on 4 June 2026 and last updated on 17 August 2026, records 466,372 full-time-equivalent teachers in England’s state-funded schools, approximately 1,900 fewer than in 2024. Qualified teacher leavers fell to 38,632 FTE, about 2,100 fewer than the previous year; the leaver rate was 8.5%. These are different populations: the total includes qualified and unqualified teachers, while the leaver measure covers qualified teachers.

Entrants exceeded leavers, but changes in working hours also matter. DfE reports a net reduction equivalent to 2,950 qualified teacher FTE from changes in working patterns. A person staying in teaching on fewer hours is not the same event as a resignation. Nor does leaving England’s state-funded sector necessarily mean abandoning education altogether. The figures therefore cannot be reduced to “more recruits minus resignations equals the total workforce change”.

Retention is a cohort measure

The retention dataset follows teachers after gaining qualified teacher status. Of the 2024 qualifying cohort, 89.7% remained in England’s state-funded schools one year later. That is not the annual retention rate for every teacher, or the percentage staying in the same school. Governors should ask which denominator a dashboard uses before comparing their school with this figure.

The recruitment pipeline and working week

The 2025/26 initial teacher training census, updated on 3 March 2026, reports 26,989 new postgraduate entrants, 12% above the revised previous year. These are provisional training entrants, not confirmed September appointments. This release also incorporates self-funded trainees into the historical series. Comparing it with an older downloaded table without checking the revised coverage risks attributing a statistical change to a recruitment improvement.

There is also evidence of reduced working hours, alongside continuing demands. In DfE’s wave 4 summary, full-time teachers reported an average 50.1 hours in their most recent full term-time week in 2025, compared with 51.2 in 2024. Full-time leaders reported 56.5 hours, down from 57.6. These are survey estimates, not contractual hours or a census measure. The full research and technical reports were added on 30 April 2026; the survey itself took place in 2025. Lower average hours do not establish why individual colleagues stay or leave.

Schoolgle’s editorial recommendation: diagnose before buying a solution

Start with a small, consistent local picture. Record staff headcount and contracted FTE separately. For departures, distinguish a move within the trust, a move to another school, retirement and a destination that is unknown. Keep personal explanations confidential. A governor report needs patterns and actions, not identifiable accounts of somebody’s health or family circumstances.

Consider a fictional two-form-entry primary. Three teachers request reduced hours and one colleague moves to a promoted post elsewhere. Calling all four “retention failures” would obscure the decisions available. A workable job-share might retain expertise; a planned leadership pathway might support succession. Equally, keeping every post filled does not demonstrate a sustainable workload if remaining colleagues repeatedly absorb unplanned cover.

For the first half-term, agree one problem to investigate with staff. If duplicated assessment recording is the concern, map the actual sequence: who enters information, who checks it, which meeting uses it and what decision follows. Trial removing one duplication. Check whether time is saved and whether teachers can still identify pupils needing support. Avoid introducing a new reporting system merely to count the burden of the old one.

Bring the findings back to governors with three items: the baseline, the change tested and the evidence of its effect. Include staff feedback and any unintended consequences. A smaller data collection that nobody trusts is not progress. A national improvement also does not excuse a deteriorating local experience. The useful leadership response to this release is a more precise question about capacity and working conditions, followed by a change that colleagues can actually notice.

send-code-practice-reform.title: SEND reform this autumn: what is starting, what remains proposed and what schools must still do
send-code-practice-reform.excerpt: Experts at Hand starts its phased rollout, while wider SEND changes remain proposals. A dated briefing on the consultation position and present responsibilities.
send-code-practice-reform.source: Schoolgle briefing · Department for Education SEND guidance and consultations
summary: Keep the current Code and existing provision separate from proposed structural reform.
Confirm the local Experts at Hand offer; it must add to EHC-plan provision.
The separate EOTAS consultation closes on 18 September 2026.

sources.title: SEND reform: putting children and young people first
SEND reform consultation portal
SEND reform consultation: HTML document
SEND Code of Practice publication
SEND Code of Practice: main statutory guidance
Experts at Hand: year-one delivery guidance
EOTAS consultation: information for parents and carers

send-code-practice-reform.body:
Schools starting the September term need two SEND plans: one for the responsibilities they already hold, and another for developments they should track. Treating every reform announcement as a new duty creates unnecessary work and can confuse families. Treating everything as distant consultation would miss support that is beginning to arrive. This briefing sets out the position checked on 7 September 2026, followed by Schoolgle’s practical recommendations.

The main consultation has closed; that is not a new Code

DfE published SEND reform: putting children and young people first on 23 February 2026. The official consultation portal records that it closed on 18 May. At this review, the publication remains labelled a closed consultation; we found no published final response on its official page. A submission deadline passing does not itself amend schools’ responsibilities.

The consultation proposals include Individual Support Plans, National Inclusion Standards and Specialist Provision Packages. These names describe the proposed future framework, not a replacement statutory checklist for this term. The document envisages phased reform and legislation. Schools should avoid telling parents that an existing entitlement has already been replaced by a proposed arrangement.

What schools must continue doing

The government still publishes the SEND Code of Practice as statutory guidance. Its listing was last updated on 12 September 2024; the linked main Code is the January 2015 document. These dates should not be presented as a newly issued “2026 Code”.

The Code’s school and EHC-plan chapters explain the existing framework: mainstream schools must use their best endeavours to secure the provision a pupil’s special educational needs require; teachers remain responsible for pupils’ progress, including when support staff are involved. SEN support follows a graduated assessment, planning, delivery and review process. Where an EHC plan is maintained, the local authority’s responsibility for securing its specified special educational provision continues, subject to the statutory exceptions. Reform publicity is not a reason to pause provision or ordinary review arrangements.

One change to investigate now: Experts at Hand

DfE’s Experts at Hand delivery guidance, published on 5 June 2026, says initial delivery begins in September 2026, with the offer expanding thereafter. It describes specialist support developed through local partnerships, rather than a promise that every school immediately receives an identical service. Crucially, this support must supplement, not substitute for, provision in an EHC plan. The guidance also says a diagnosis must not be a prerequisite for access.

Our interpretation for school leaders is to ask the local authority how the first-year offer can be accessed, which settings and needs it initially prioritises, and who will communicate referral decisions. Do not announce a particular specialist, response time or allocation until the local arrangements are confirmed. Record what is available, what has been requested and what remains unresolved.

A separate consultation still needs attention

The EOTAS consultation information for families, updated on 14 July, gives a closing date of 18 September 2026. It covers education otherwise than at school, health-related absence and online alternative provision. DfE says decisions have not been made and that any changes would start from September 2030 at the earliest, subject to Parliament. Do not confuse this continuing exercise with an outcome from the broader consultation that closed in May.

Schoolgle’s editorial recommendation: make the transition understandable

Give the SENCO, headteacher and relevant governor a shared one-page change log. Use three headings: current responsibilities, confirmed local implementation, and proposals awaiting decisions. Each entry needs an owner, a dated source and the next review point. A national announcement belongs in a different category from written confirmation that a service is available to your school.

For a practical example, imagine a pupil who finds multi-step classroom instructions difficult. The useful record is the barrier observed, the adaptation agreed with the family and pupil, who will use it, and what will be reviewed. “Referred for support” is an action, not evidence that the child can now participate more confidently. Ask staff to bring a small sample of work or a specific observation to the review, rather than creating another lengthy narrative.

For governors, separate delivery from aspiration. Ask whether agreed support happened, whether families understand the next step and whether unresolved gaps have a named escalation route. Keep case-level details within appropriate confidential channels. The immediate opportunity is better coordination around actual children; the longer-term task is to prepare for reforms without presenting proposals as settled rights, guarantees or duties.

governance-handbook-changes-2026.title: Governance in 2026: use the right guide and ask sharper questions
governance-handbook-changes-2026.excerpt: A practical briefing for maintained-school governors and academy trustees.
governance-handbook-changes-2026.body:
Governors have limited meeting time. A pack full of information is only useful if it helps them identify what needs scrutiny and what happens next.

DfE publishes separate governance guides for maintained schools and academy trusts. Begin with the guide for your structure. The old article's general Governance Handbook wording has been updated; the URL is retained for existing readers.

Check the relevant source

The maintained-schools guide was updated in July 2026. Academy trustees should use the academy trust governance guide alongside applicable trust requirements. Do not assume a statement about one structure transfers unchanged to another.

Turn the report into questions

Our suggested agenda note is short: the decision or assurance needed, the evidence, the main uncertainty and the next review. Ask what changed since the previous meeting and which action needs board attention.

If a chart shows improvement, ask about the period, denominator and comparison. If a risk is marked green, ask what evidence supports that assessment.

Keep the follow-through

Record the decision, owner and date for returning to it. Distinguish a question answered from an action completed. The minutes should allow someone absent from the meeting to understand the reasoning.

Schoolgle's governance tools organise people, meetings and records. Good governance still depends on informed challenge, proportionate evidence and leaders being able to explain what is happening in school.

school-budget-benchmarking-2026.title: School budget benchmarking in 2026: turn comparisons into better decisions
school-budget-benchmarking-2026.excerpt: IFS, DfE and NFER describe different parts of the financial picture. A practical briefing on dated forecasts, meaningful comparators and school-level decisions.
school-budget-benchmarking-2026.source: IFS, Department for Education and NFER
summary: National funding and cost models do not establish a particular school’s spending capacity.
Check the reporting period, unit and comparator group before interpreting a difference.
Connect each proposed financial action to provision, evidence and an explicit review point.

sources.title: Annual report on education spending in England: 2025–26
Schools’ costs: technical note — Schools' costs 2025 to 2029
Schools financial value standard (SFVS): checklist guidance
School Teacher Labour Market in England Annual Report 2026

school-budget-benchmarking-2026.body:
A national funding headline and a school's forecast answer different questions. In September 2026, school leaders in England need to understand both, while avoiding the temptation to treat a comparator's spending level as the right budget for their own pupils. A useful benchmarking discussion ends with a better question, a checked assumption or a considered decision. A red indicator alone is none of those.

What the national evidence actually says

The IFS 2025–26 education spending report, published in January 2026, estimated that total school spending per pupil had returned to its 2010–11 level. That broad recovery did not mean equivalent growth in mainstream resources: over half of the real-terms funding increase between 2019–20 and 2025–26 was explained by SEND spending. IFS estimated mainstream funding per pupil grew by 5% over that period. These are England-level findings, not a forecast for an individual school.

DfE's March Schools' costs technical note takes a different analytical approach. Its central estimate of £1 billion of national financial headroom across 2026–27 and 2027–28 excluded the coming teacher and support-staff pay awards, which were undecided when the note was written. Only around a quarter of that modelled headroom related to 2026–27. The document explicitly warns against reading national averages as individual-school results. This is a dated modelling exercise, not £1 billion of uncommitted money schools can now spend.

Schoolgle's interpretation is that a September review should replace earlier planning assumptions wherever confirmed allocations, payroll information or contract terms are available. Keep unresolved assumptions visible. Do not present a January or March forecast as the latest settled pay decision, and do not silently add a separate grant when it has already been included in the school's confirmed funding.

Compare the right thing

The current Schools Financial Value Standard checklist guidance points to the Financial Benchmarking and Insights Tool. It distinguishes comparators based on pupil characteristics from those based on building characteristics: premises and utilities costs may depend more on the estate than pupil intake. For maintained schools, it describes annual benchmarking and reporting findings to governors. That is a reason to investigate differences carefully, rather than treat the middle of a chart as a universal spending target.

Before discussing an outlier, write down the reporting year, population and unit being compared. Is it pounds per pupil, percentage of expenditure or an absolute total? Has the school changed size since the reported period? Are central trust services recorded consistently? The answers belong alongside the chart so that the same explanation does not have to be reconstructed at every committee meeting.

A worked question, not a predetermined saving

Consider a fictional primary school whose premises spending per pupil is higher than its comparison group. A proposed review could separate energy consumption, unit prices, cleaning coverage and one-off repairs. If roll numbers have fallen while the building remains the same size, the ratio can rise without a comparable increase in total spending. That arithmetic does not prove spending is efficient; it identifies a question that a per-pupil chart cannot resolve.

The team might discover an unusual repair year, a contract approaching renewal or avoidable consumption outside opening hours. Each would lead to a different response. Record the explanation, evidence still needed, responsible colleague and decision date. If no change is justified, record that conclusion too. Benchmarking should permit a reasoned decision to retain provision.

Keep staffing decisions connected to provision

NFER's March 2026 teacher labour-market report found improving recruitment and retention indicators, while secondary recruitment remained below target and workload perceptions remained less positive than for comparable workers. Its findings caution against assuming recruitment difficulties have disappeared. They provide workforce context, rather than a recommended staffing percentage for a particular school.

Our suggested finance-meeting pack therefore puts the curriculum and planned provision beside the staffing forecast. Show which assumptions drive the result, which roles or contracts could change, and what consequences would need assessment before any decision. Test a small number of locally relevant scenarios, such as a different intake or an extended vacancy, rather than applying an arbitrary savings percentage across departments.

Keep the forecast outturn, cash position and reserves distinct. Give governors a short explanation of the movement since the last forecast, the action proposed and the uncertainty that remains. The outcome should be a shared account of the school's position, supported by current records and professional judgement. National research helps frame the challenge; it cannot decide the right trade-offs for your pupils.

siams-inspection-readiness.title: SIAMS: connect your school's vision to lived experience
siams-inspection-readiness.excerpt: Use the current framework and look for the explanation behind the evidence.
siams-inspection-readiness.body:
A vision statement is easy to find on a website. Explaining how it shapes daily school life takes a different kind of conversation.

The National Society for Education publishes SIAMS inspection materials, including a September 2026 framework. Check the version relevant to your inspection and work with your diocesan support. Do not treat an Ofsted checklist as a substitute.

Start with a real decision

Our suggestion is to choose a decision about school life and explain how the school's vision influenced it. What did leaders consider? What happened? Whose experience helps you evaluate it?

A useful example can include difficulty or a change of mind. Evidence does not become stronger because the account avoids every complication.

Listen beyond the document

Gather perspectives through normal school processes. Consider whether pupils, staff and families recognise the experience described by leaders. Keep examples grounded and handle personal information appropriately.

A display or policy may explain an intention. It does not on its own establish the experience of the people in school.

Keep the review connected

Link the question, evidence, conclusion and next action. Make ownership clear. Revisit whether the action helped, rather than simply marking it complete.

Schoolgle can support organising evidence and follow-up. The school's evaluation of its Christian vision and the inspection framework require knowledgeable human interpretation. Use the current official materials as the authority for what inspectors consider.

ai-expert-work-schools.title: AI and expert work: keep the review where it matters
ai-expert-work-schools.excerpt: Where an assistant can help, and why responsibility still needs a person.
ai-expert-work-schools.body:
An assistant can produce a convincing first draft remarkably quickly. That changes how some work starts. It does not remove the need to understand what the draft says.

The DfE publishes guidance on generative AI in education. Schools should consider the particular use case, data and safeguards rather than treating every AI task as equivalent.

Find a bounded job

Our suggestion is to begin with work where a person can readily check the result: reorganising a public document, drafting a general explanation or suggesting an agenda. Keep the source available and make the review part of the task.

Do not confuse fluent writing with knowledge of your school. An assistant may fill a gap with a plausible invention unless the information and limits are made explicit.

Design the handoff

Name who reviews the output and what they must check. Facts, dates, audience, tone and missing context all matter. For sensitive work, approval of the tool and data use comes before the prompt.

Some decisions have consequences an assistant cannot own. Safeguarding, employment and decisions about individual pupils require the appropriate professional process.

Measure the finished job

Count the time needed to check and correct the draft, not just the time needed to generate it. Notice whether the work became clearer or simply longer.

Schoolgle's view is practical: let AI help with the legwork and keep the judgement visible. A useful assistant should make it easier for people to do responsible work, not obscure who is accountable.

intelligence-not-software.title: When a dashboard should lead to a decision
intelligence-not-software.excerpt: The useful step between seeing a number and knowing what to investigate.
intelligence-not-software.body:
A dashboard says a measure has fallen. Everyone can see the colour changed. The difficult question is what the team should do with that information.

Explain the number first

Our starting point is the source, date, group and definition. Has the measure changed, or has the group changed? Are the figures comparable? Does a missing value mean no data or no concern?

These details can look less exciting than a chart, but they determine whether the conversation rests on something solid. Keep uncertainty visible rather than smoothing it away in a summary.

Make the next question specific

A pattern may justify investigation without establishing a cause. Invite the people closest to the work to add context. Consider alternative explanations before recommending an intervention.

For example, a cohort comparison might prompt a review of assessment coverage. That is different from concluding that teaching has become less effective.

Connect the decision to a review

If the school chooses an action, name the owner, intended change and evidence for review. The EEF implementation process provides a useful structure for thinking beyond launch to delivery and sustaining a change.

Later, ask whether the action happened and whether the evidence supports continuing it. A completed task and an improved outcome are separate claims.

This is the direction behind Schoolgle: sources, questions, actions and follow-through connected in one working account. The value is not another narrative generated from the same figures. It is helping a team understand what it knows and decide what to do next.
